Name once, then she, he, they

After the first mention, use the pronoun. Bring the name back only when it is unclear who you mean, or when you compare two people.

Does Lena like her job? Yes, she does.

Depois da primeira menção, use o pronome. O nome volta só quando não está claro de quem você fala, ou quando você compara duas pessoas.

1
Profile

From the tram to the finish line

Do bonde à linha de chegada
Past, present perfect, present continuous, plans

Lena Hoffmann used to hate running. For twenty years she took the tram everywhere, and she was always the last one to finish the run in gym class. Then, in 2019, her doctor told her to exercise, and Lena signed up for a beginners’ group in Vienna. She had never run more than two hundred meters before, so her first weeks were hard. She was getting up at six every morning, and she often wanted to quit.

Today things are different. The group has grown a lot: it now has forty members, and Lena has just finished a half marathon in Lisbon. Her bright orange shoes are famous in the club, and her teammates are taking photos of them before every race. Her brother Jonas drives her to the races on weekends. He says Lena is training too much, but she doesn’t agree.

Next year she is going to lead a beginners’ group for older people. She hopes the city will give her a small grant for it. If the group grows, she will probably start a weekly race for the whole neighborhood.

Not everything is easy. Last winter Lena injured her knee twice, and she had to rest for six weeks. She also bought new shoes, which cost more than two hundred euros. Her teammates were very kind: some of them brought her soup while she waited for the knee to heal. She says that she has never regretted joining the group, although she sometimes misses sleeping late on Sundays. When she was young, she wanted to be a pianist, but she was afraid of performing.

Email · work

Changes at the warehouse

Mudanças no galpão
Passive, modals, future, present perfect

Dear team,

As you know, the warehouse has been using the same system for twelve years. Starting March 3, a new scanning system will be introduced, and every employee must complete a training session before that date. The sessions are being organized by Ingrid Larsen, our operations manager, and they will take place on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons in the meeting room.

The new system was chosen after a six-month test in our Rotterdam branch. During the test, the workers there reported 30 percent fewer errors, and deliveries arrived faster. Some of you have asked whether the old scanners will be thrown away. They won’t: they are going to be sent to our smaller warehouse in Warsaw.

Because of the changes, the night shift can’t start at 10 p.m. during the first week. It will start at midnight instead. Anyone who needs help with the schedule should talk to Ingrid before Friday. If we receive enough feedback, we may adjust the training next month.

A few practical details. The training lasts about ninety minutes, and snacks will be provided at every session. If you can’t attend your session, please tell your supervisor as soon as possible so that another date can be arranged. New employees, who started this month, will be trained separately by me. We have also asked a technician, who has worked with this system for years, to be available during the first two weeks.

Thank you for your patience.
Tomasz Nowak, Director of Logistics

Story

The flight that never left

O voo que nunca decolou
Past simple, past continuous, past perfect, reported speech

Last October, Ama and her brother Kofi were supposed to fly from London to Accra for their cousin’s wedding. They had packed the night before, and they arrived at Heathrow Airport three hours early. While they were waiting at the gate, the screen suddenly changed: the flight had been delayed because of a storm.

At first nobody was worried. Ama was reading a book, and Kofi was talking to a man who sold coffee near the gate. After two hours, though, the airline announced that the flight was canceled. By then, the airport had become very crowded, and a lot of passengers were shouting at the staff.

Ama decided to call her cousin, but her phone had died. Fortunately, Kofi had brought a charger. When she finally got through, her cousin said that the wedding would start at eleven the next morning, so there was still a chance. The airline put them on an early flight the next morning. They slept for four hours at a hotel near the airport, and they landed in Accra at nine.

Ama still remembers the taxi driver, who drove so fast that she closed her eyes. They arrived at the church with only twenty minutes to spare.

The wedding itself was beautiful. Their cousin, who had been planning it for two years, cried when she saw them in the church. Later, during the party, Kofi danced with an old aunt, while Ama was telling the whole family about the storm. Nobody could believe that they had made it. The next day, the airline sent an email offering them a travel voucher, but Ama said she would rather keep the story.

Magazine article

Why are so many adults sleeping less?

Por que tantos adultos estão dormindo menos?
Present simple, present continuous, present perfect, modals of advice

Doctors say that adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep, but a recent survey of 2,000 Australians shows that almost half of them sleep less than six hours a night. Researchers believe that smartphones are partly responsible. According to Dr. Mei Tanaka, who leads a sleep clinic in Osaka, people are checking their phones in bed more than ever, and the blue light makes it harder to fall asleep.

Work also plays a role. Many employees now answer messages after dinner, and some of them have been working from home since the pandemic, so the line between work and rest has disappeared. Dr. Tanaka has treated more than three hundred patients with insomnia in the last five years, and she says the problem is growing every year.

There are simple things you can do. Most experts recommend going to bed at the same time every day and keeping the bedroom dark and cool. You shouldn’t drink coffee after four in the afternoon, and you ought to put your phone in another room. Some people also take a short walk after dinner, which can help the body relax. However, if you sleep badly for more than a month, you should see a doctor. Sleep is not a luxury: a tired person makes more mistakes, gets sick more often, and enjoys life less.

Not everyone agrees on the solution. Some researchers have argued that companies should stop sending emails after six o’clock, and a few countries are already discussing laws about it. Others believe that schools should start later, because teenagers usually fall asleep late and need more rest in the morning. In a small town in Norway, where classes began at nine thirty last year, students’ grades improved and absences fell by twelve percent. If the results continue, similar experiments will be tried in other regions.

News report

A neighborhood fights for its library

Um bairro luta pela sua biblioteca
Conditionals, reported speech, passive, going to

The Eastfield library in Auckland, which opened in 1974, may have to close next summer. The city council announced last week that it would cut the budget for public libraries by forty percent. According to the mayor, the money is needed for a new bus terminal, which is going to be built near the river.

Residents have reacted strongly. Last Saturday, about two hundred people gathered in front of the library, and a retired teacher named Ngozi Adeyemi told the crowd that she had learned to read there as a child. “If the library closes, the children in this area will have nowhere to study,” she said. A local student, whose mother cleans the library, has started an online petition. It has already been signed by more than nine thousand people.

Not everyone supports the petition. A shop owner on the same street, who has never visited the library, told a reporter that the money could be used better. “I like books,” he said, “but I like new roads more.” The mayor’s office has not commented on his words. Meanwhile, the library staff is organizing a reading night next Friday, and the first fifty visitors will receive a free book.

The council says it has not made a final decision. If enough people signed the petition, the mayor said, she would consider another solution. One idea is to move the library into the old post office, which has been empty for years. Volunteers have offered to paint the walls and carry the books themselves, and a bookshop owner has promised to donate a hundred new titles. If the council agreed, the library could reopen in September. Everyone is now waiting to hear what will happen at Thursday’s meeting.
